shared_genus_recognition.look_here_first: Green hawthorn: a small thorny Rosaceae tree with alternate simple finely serrated small blades, sometimes weakly lobed (0–3 lobes/side), white five-petal blossoms with many stamens, and clustered small RED pomes with stone-like pyrenes. Species key needs thorn placement + leaves + fruit/flowers together; Crataegus hybridization and cultivar selection frustrate shortcuts.
shared_genus_recognition.identity_warning: Source-pool reference only, exact-species full scientific review and range status handled separately

genus_comparison_matrix.reference_contrast: Compare botanical thorn (branch) with Rosa/Rubus epidermal prickles; not every twig has a thorn.

genus_comparison_matrix.source_taxon: Alternate simple leaves 2–6(–7) cm, variable oval/oblong/rhombic shape, serrations and often no lobes or 1–3 per side

genus_comparison_matrix.source_taxon: Clusters of white five-petaled flowers, numerous stamens and inferior ovary within Rosaceae hypanthium

look_here_first_sequence: Recognize plant architecture and leaf arrangement before flower color.
Compare leaf shape, insertion and microstructures on several mature samples.
Inspect floral anatomy under magnification and track into mature fruit.
Cross-check the strongest lookalike with matched scale; avoid uncertain species IDs.
Respect the source-name/canonical manifest boundary and keep nonlocal native labels unchanged.
scientific_cautions: Source-pool C. viridis currently uninstalled; genus text is identification reference, not a confirmed target-zone native claim.
Species of hawthorn notoriously variable with reproductive hybrids and horticultural 'Winter King' selection; ornamental planting cannot prove wild specimen identity.
Some hawthorn species vary thorn number and leaf lobing; do not make a hard key from one red haw or one spine.
Rosaceae fruit terminology: pome-like accessory fruit and hard pyrenes, not aggregate Rubus drupelets.

look_here_first: FIRST decide if a thorny woody tree has ALTERNATE simple toothed leaves, then see if its mature leaf has 1–4 lobes per side. On flowering twig, LOOK AT THE ANTHERS, not petal color: Texas Hawthorn (C. texana) has ca. 20 ROSE/PURPLE anthers and fuzzy flower cups; Downy Hawthorn (C. mollis) has cream anthers; Green Hawthorn (C. viridis) has ivory/cream anthers and mostly glabrous flower cups. Brazos Hawthorn (C. brazoria) shares colored anthers, but usually has unlobed/weakly lobed elliptic leaves. Fruit size/stone count corroborate; thorn presence alone is not proof.

texana_diagnostic_comparison.lesson: Texas hawthorn — pink anthers plus lobed leaves
texana_diagnostic_comparison.look_here_first: Texas hawthorn vs Brazos: BOTH can have ROSE-colored anthers and 20 stamens; TEXANA typically 1–4 leaf lobes per side, BRAZORIA usually no conspicuous lobes. Texas vs Downy and Green: purple/rose versus cream/ivory anthers; check woolly flower cups and fruit size.

comparison_matrix.texana: 4–7 cm rhombic/ovate, 1–4 lobes each side and coarse serrations
comparison_matrix.brazoria: 4–7 cm mostly elliptic, unlobed or tiny apicula on sides
comparison_matrix.mollis: Broad leaf often lobed 2–4 per side; VERY similar
comparison_matrix.viridis: More variable narrow oval to rhombic, often weakly lobed; leaf alone not decisive

comparison_matrix.texana: Usually 20 stamens with PINK, ROSE-PURPLE, RED or PURPLE anthers
comparison_matrix.brazoria: Usually 20 stamens with ROSE anthers (same colored group)
comparison_matrix.viridis: 20 stamens, usually CREAM/IVORY anthers (rare colored outliers)

comparison_matrix.texana: Hypanthium and new shoots densely woolly/tomentose
comparison_matrix.brazoria: Hypanthium and new shoots also woolly
comparison_matrix.mollis: Dense woolly floral cup as texana
comparison_matrix.viridis: Usually GLABROUS flower cups, twigs relatively smooth; some hairy variants exist

comparison_matrix.texana: Red, usually 9–14 mm (up to 25), 4–5 hard inner stones
comparison_matrix.brazoria: Red to yellow/orange, often 8–12 mm, 4–5 stones
comparison_matrix.viridis: Usually orange to deep red, smaller 5–8 mm, 3–5 stones

comparison_matrix.texana: Some long straight twigs thorns ~4–5 cm, sometimes absent
comparison_matrix.brazoria: Often few or none, potentially 4–7 cm
comparison_matrix.viridis: Variable; cannot key by presence alone

best_three_part_check: Compare mature short-shoot leaves with same magnification/ruler, NOT juvenile extension-shoot leaves
Count anthers (note color) and photograph hypanthium hairs on open fresh blooms
Confirm ripe fruit dimension plus hard pyrene count
texana_diagnostic_comparison.memory_rule: TEXANA = LOBES + ROSE ANTHERS + WOOLLY flower cups. BRAZORIA = LESS LOBES + ROSE ANTHERS. MOLLIS/VIRIDIS = typically CREAM ANTHERS.
texana_diagnostic_comparison.variety_note: FNA C. texana var. texana often 2–4 deeper lobes per side; var. dasyphylla often 1–2 shallower lobes per side. Variation overlaps; not new species cards.

field_vocabulary.anther: AN-ther — pollen-making tip of a stamen; pink-purple versus cream helps separate species
field_vocabulary.hypanthium: high-PAN-thee-um — outer flower cup enclosing flower base; fuzzy vs smooth can identify hawthorn
field_vocabulary.tomentose: toh-MEN-tose — thickly covered with soft, short hairs
field_vocabulary.pome: POHM — small apple-like fruit; not a single-stone plum
field_vocabulary.pyrene: PIE-reen — hard stone-like seed enclosure inside a haw
field_vocabulary.lobe: A separate outward section of the one leaf blade, divided by a notch
field_vocabulary.corymb: KOR-imb — a cluster with flower tops at similar height
